title: This Hormone May Explain Why Exercise Helps the Brain
paragraphs: Research has shown that exercise isn't just good for your body — it's great for your brain as well. However, scientists are still looking into exactly why.

One thing scientists are looking at is a hormone called irisin, which is released by muscles during exercise. And a new Australian study looked at how strength training might affect irisin levels and brain health in older adults.
The research team followed 24 healthy adults over the age of 65 as they took part in a 12-week strength-training program.

The researchers measured the levels of irisin in participants' blood before their first workout, then again immediately after the workout, as well as 30 minutes and 60 minutes later. They took the same set of measurements at the time of the participants' last workout 12 weeks later.

The researchers also tested participants' memory and verbal fluency. In verbal fluency tests, people are given a limited time to say as many words as they can think of in a certain category, such as fruits, or words starting with the letter Q.

After their first workout, the participants showed big increases in their irisin levels. But their final workout didn't produce such large amounts of irisin. And even after the 12-week program, there was no change in their irisin levels when at rest.
That might sound like the exercise had no real effect.
However, the researchers did find that changes in participants' memory were linked to their levels of irisin at the start of the study, and also to how high their irisin levels went after exercising.
And, more interestingly, even though irisin levels didn't stay high, the researchers found that participants' verbal fluency improved by the end of the training program.
This suggests that even repeated, short-term increases in irisin could be enough to improve brain health in the long term.
